title: Thus have I heard
hookLine: the cousin who remembered everything; most discourses begin with his words
carry: a letter with an address attached

cards: "Thus have I heard." Open the long discourses in the Victorian English of Rhys Davids, and those are the first words you meet. Turn the page to the next discourse, and there they are again.
Then a place: at one time the Blessed One was staying near such-and-such a town, in such-and-such a grove. Then the teaching. The same small doorway, discourse after discourse.
And the obvious question: who is the I? Who heard?

teach.b: Tradition gives one answer: Ananda. He was, tradition says, the Buddha's cousin, and for a long stretch his personal attendant, close at hand when the Buddha taught.
In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of foremost disciples, the qualities named for him include great learning and a good memory. So the I is the man who remembered.
A story a few days from now tells how he came to say these words aloud for the whole community. Now look at what the phrase does. First, it's a witness, not an author.
Not, I teach. Not even, the Buddha taught. Just: this is what I heard.
The speaker steps aside and points to someone else.
Second, it fixes the scene. After it comes where the Buddha was staying, and often who came to him and why. The teaching arrives with an address attached, like a letter.
Heard is a modest verb. It admits that what follows passed through one person's ears and memory. Some readers hear humility in it; others hear a claim of reliability: I was there.
Both can be true at once. Fourth, it kept going. The opening shows up in sutras of later traditions too, in Sanskrit and Chinese, the Diamond Sutra among them.

teach.h: THE FRONT DOOR OF A LIBRARY.
teach.b: One person's careful listening became the front door of a library.
And none of it would exist if someone hadn't paid attention in the room and kept what he heard without improving it.

how: When Buddhist discourses are chanted, in Pali in Theravada communities and in Chinese, Tibetan or Japanese in others, the chant often begins with the words 'thus have I heard' in that language.

o: the Buddha's son, who joined as a young boy
the first monk to understand the teaching
the cousin and attendant who remembered the talks

games.q: thus have I heard: tap the pairs.

s: 'thus have I heard' means the Buddha is speaking
it's a listener speaking: this is what I heard. tradition says it's Ananda.
the list of foremost disciples names good memory among Ananda's qualities
only the Pali discourses open this way
later sutras in Sanskrit and Chinese, the Diamond Sutra among them, open the same way.

games.q: you heard the teacher give a talk, and now a gathering asks you to repeat it. how do you begin?
o: let me improve on what he said.
games.why: the discourses open with a witness's words: thus have I heard. then where, and to whom. tradition says the speaker is Ananda.

practice: Go back to one sentence someone said to you in the last day or two, something that mattered even a little, and try to hear it exactly, word for word, with the place and the voice around it.
If the words blur, don't fill the gap with your own; just say to yourself, this much I heard.

wordCard.voice: Ananda. The one tradition credits as the witness behind every discourse's opening, thus have I heard, remembering what he heard, where, and from whom. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: thus by me heard, the opening of the discourses; Sanskrit sutras say evam maya shrutam.

carryVoice: Your line: a letter with an address attached. Who heard, where, and then the teaching. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1 (opening words), Dialogues of the Buddha
